title: What is a pre listing inspection
description: What is a pre listing inspection? A paid report before you advertise, separate from the walk you do yourself and from the buyer's later inspection.
summary: It is an optional written look you buy so you can repair, disclose, or reprice before a buyer is on a deadline.
body: What is a pre listing inspection? It is a home inspector's report that you order before you list, so the findings arrive while you still control the calendar. It is not required for an ordinary sale. It is not the [Pre-listing walkthrough](/tips/walk-the-house-before-you-hire), which is the slow walk you do with a notepad and no fee. Do that walk first. Hire the inspector when you want a named method and a file you can hand to a buyer.

A general inspection is not a roof certification, a sewer scope, a pest letter, or an engineer's foundation report. Ask what the fee excludes before you book. If your walk already shows a foundation symptom, the foundation guide comes before you pay a generalist to recommend an engineer. Attend the visit. Comments in the hallway sometimes never reach the summary page.

The buyer's inspector can still write a different list. Lenders order appraisals, which are another visit entirely. Your report does not bind them. It binds you, in the sense that you now know what it says. If your state form asks about known conditions, a report you paid for is something you know. Ask your agent or a local attorney before you withhold pages. Do not edit the file down to the cheerful half.

The guide on this topic is the decision and the timing. This note is the definition: a paid, written, pre-listing look that you sort into fix, disclose, or leave. A verbal stroll with no document is a conversation. Call it an inspection only when the report has a name on it. Schedule it while you can still change the price or the repairs, not the morning the photographer arrives.
steps: Finish your own walkthrough and mark fix, disclose, or leave.
Ask the inspector what the fee includes and what it does not.
Attend the visit and keep the full report.
Sort the findings the same way you sorted your walk.
Expect the buyer to hire their own inspector anyway.

title: Pre listing inspection cost
description: Pre listing inspection cost is the inspector's quote, often in a typical range of a few hundred dollars, plus extra fees for sewer, roof, or structure.
summary: Get the general-inspection quote and the specialist quotes separately, and type the ones you accept into the net sheet.
body: Pre listing inspection cost is a quote, not a national fee schedule. A typical range for a general home inspection is often about $300 to $600, and higher when the house is large or the visit is long. A sewer scope, a roof letter, or a foundation engineer is extra. A typical range for a simple specialist visit is often about $150 to $400. These are labels so you can tell a small invoice from a project. Your written quotes are the budget.

Ask what the number includes: the visit, the written report, and a return call. A low quote that is only a walk with no file is not the same product. A quote that promises to waive the buyer's inspection is not a product you should buy. No inspector can promise that. Put the invoices you accept into the [net proceeds calculator](/tools/net-proceeds) beside any repairs you choose. The fee is small next to a repair bid and large next to zero if you were not going to use the report.

Do not add a specialist you do not need because the menu offered it. Do add the specialist your own eyes already flagged. Paying $450 to be told the roof needs a roofer, when you can see missing tabs, is only useful if the report helps you disclose or sequence the work. The cost note stops at the invoice. Whether the fee is worth it is the next note.

Get two quotes if the first one surprises you, on the same scope. A price that includes a thermal camera and a price that does not are different visits. Write the difference down. Then book the date while you still have time to repair or reprice. A report that arrives after the photographer has left can still help the disclosure. It will not help the photos.
steps: Ask two inspectors what a general report costs for this house.
List specialist fees only for systems your walk already questioned.
Reject any quote that claims it replaces the buyer's inspection.
Enter the accepted fees and repair bids on the net sheet.
Book a date that leaves time to act on the report.

title: Pre listing inspection checklist
description: A pre listing inspection checklist: walk the house yourself, book the inspector, read the full report, and decide what to fix, disclose, or leave.
summary: Use a short list so the report becomes a decision instead of a stack of paper on the counter.
body: A pre listing inspection checklist is the sequence around the visit, not a second copy of the inspector's form. Start with the [Pre-listing walkthrough](/tips/walk-the-house-before-you-hire). One line per fault. Then call the inspector with that list in hand so you can ask them to spend time where you already have a question. Book a day that is not the photo day and not the day a plumber is still cutting.

On the visit, open the areas you will be asked about later: the attic access if it is safe to use, the electrical panel, the furnace, and the sinks. You are not performing the inspection. You are making sure the inspector can see what a buyer will see. Take your own notes beside theirs. When the report arrives, sort every major line into fix, disclose, or leave. [What to fix before selling a house](/tips/fix-function-before-finish) is the order for the lines you mark fix: water and function before paint.

Put bids on the fix lines and the numbers into the net sheet. Decide whether the full report goes to buyers. If you give it, give all of it. File it in the closing folder with the receipts for work you finish. Tell the photographer which repairs will be done before the shoot and which will be disclosed instead. The listing should match the file.

Leave a line on the checklist for the buyer's future inspection. You are not done when your report is filed. You are prepared. A second list can still arrive. The offers guide is where you answer it in writing. This checklist ends when your own report has an owner, a sort, and a place in the folder. Leave room on the list for a buyer's later inspection so you are not surprised that a second report exists.
steps: Complete your own walk and send the questions with the booking.
Schedule the visit away from photos and open repairs.
Sort the report into fix, disclose, or leave.
File the full report and the receipts together.
Match the listing photos and the disclosure to that file.

title: Is a pre listing inspection worth it
description: Is a pre listing inspection worth it? Compare the quote with the repairs it lets you choose on your calendar, not with a promise of a higher price.
summary: It is worth the fee when you will use the report to repair, disclose, or reprice. It is optional when your walk is already clear.
body: Is a pre listing inspection worth it? Only if you will act on the paper. A report you ignore is an expense. A report that lets you fix a leak and disclose an old stain, before a buyer has a deadline, can be cheaper than a credit fight in the option period or the inspection window. This site does not promise the fee comes back in the sale price. Nobody honest can promise that.

Compare the quote with the size of the surprises you are trying to move earlier. On a house you have lived in and walked carefully, the walkthrough may be enough, and you can negotiate whatever a buyer later finds. On a house you do not know well, including one you inherited, the fee buys a method you do not have. The inherited-house guide still comes first if you are not sure you may even sell. An inspection does not create authority.

Count the specialists. A $450 general report plus two $250 add-ons is a different decision from the general report alone. A typical range is a label. Your quotes are the test. If the money is tight against the payoff, read the mortgage note before you add optional visits. A shortage at closing is not improved by another PDF.

Skip it when you want to, and write that you skipped it so the choice was deliberate. Do not skip your own walk. That walk is free and it is the page this topic keeps pointing at. Hire the inspector when the written file will change your price, your repairs, or your disclosure, and you have time to use it. Write the decision down so a later week does not reopen it by accident.
steps: Write what you would do differently if the report found a leak.
If the answer is nothing, do not buy the report yet.
If the answer is repair, disclose, or reprice, get quotes.
Add specialist fees only where your walk already raised a question.
Do the free walkthrough either way.
